video.title: 3 Tips to Rip the Low Backhand

classification.reason: The coach gives specific executable cues including dipping the back knee deep, hinging at the hips with a straight back, and shoving the hands forward through the ball past the front foot.

problem.title_as_question: How can you rip and attack the low backhand?
problem.definition: Executing an aggressive, offensive two-handed backhand on low balls by establishing balance and drive with a deep back knee, tilting the torso via hip hinge, and extending the hands forward through contact.

quotes.text: All right, we're going to go over three fundamentals that will help you rip the low backhand.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: The first one is this back knee, and I want you to see just how deep that is.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: We need to get this knee deep for balance purposes and so we can use it to drive through the ball.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: If the ball gets on top of you, you're going to have to mostly just use your hands and upper body,
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: if you can get just a little bit of distance, you can press through that knee, press that back foot through towards your target,
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: you'll see Alexa do it here a couple times where she's able to slide that foot forward. That's really what we want.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: You need a strong quad, strong knee to do this. And this knee is out over the toe here.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: That is the most athletic, most efficient way to play this ball. So, that's the first to dip this back knee.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: A lot of rec players when they hit this shot, they're a lot straighter than they think.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: They might think they're bending the knee, but they are not really sitting down into this deep knee bend position that's necessary
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: The second fundamental we're going to talk about is the angle of the torso.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Now, her back is straight. Her back is is erect. It's not curved.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: She's not bent over in the sense that her back is curved, but her hips are hinged, and that allows her racket path to go more low to high than usual.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: When you tilt like this, that makes your hands naturally go low to high with the same biomechanically efficient swing that you always use.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: So, we have to dip the back knee. We also have to tilt the torso, hinge at the hips, back straight.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: We're not bending over like curling over, but tilt the torso, hinge at the hips. That's how you attack these low balls
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: and get the hands to fly up when you throw them out away from your body like you normally do.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: For our third fundamental, we're going to use the side view. This is the same set of backhands.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: So, if you look at her front foot there, her hands are clearing her front foot every stroke.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: A lot of people on the two-handed backhand get a little confused. We don't finish over our shoulder because we're yanking the racket over our shoulder.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: We throw the racket forward. We drive the racket forward. And then by coincidence, it often finishes over the shoulder, but not always.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: I just want you to see in relation to the front foot just how much the hands extend through the shot, extend through this contact.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Take the hands, shove them forward, forward, forward through the ball.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: They should clear your front foot on it pretty much every single backhand you hit.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Yeah, that's good execution there. I probably need to practice this more when I play.
quotes.speaker: coach

symptoms.description: The player hits the low ball while standing significantly straighter than they realize without a deep knee bend.
The player curls or rounds the back over instead of tilting the torso with hinged hips and an erect spine.
The hands yank upward across the shoulder rather than extending well forward beyond the front foot.

causes.statement: Recreational players remain too upright instead of sitting down into a deep back knee bend necessary for balance and driving through the ball.
Players curl the spine instead of hinging at the hips with a straight back and tilting the torso forward, preventing a natural low-to-high swing path.
Players yank the racket upward across the shoulder instead of throwing and extending their hands forward through the shot.

angles.summary: Hinging at the hips and tilting the torso allows the hands to swing low to high naturally while preserving the player's standard swing mechanics.
Finishing over the shoulder on a two-handed backhand is an incidental byproduct of driving forward, not the goal of an intentional upward yank.
Recreational players often feel like they are bending their knees when they are actually far more erect than required.
Alexa demonstrates an athletic low position with the knee tracked over the toe, loading the quadriceps, and sliding the back foot forward.

solutions.summary: Maintain spacing from the ball, dip the back knee deep, and press through that knee to drive the back foot toward the target.
solutions.external_goal: press that back foot through towards your target

solutions.summary: Tilt the torso and hinge deeply at the hips while keeping the back straight and erect rather than curling over the ball.
Drive and shove the hands forward through the ball on contact so they visibly clear past the front foot.
solutions.external_goal: shove them forward, forward, forward through the ball
